title: Inside a black hole? What the sources predict—and why this route closed

cards.heading: This route closed because it had no calibrated, identifying target
cards.narration: Could our universe be inside a black hole? This is Duho's personal interest, outside the lab's research programme. We read primary sources for their predictions. One branch gives neutron stars a number to check. For galaxy spin, the sources give no expected size for the effect, and a measurement could not identify a black-hole origin. So this route closes. The idea is not declared true or false.
cards.diagram: Three-column verdict map. Left: PERSONAL INTEREST badge above a plain nested-horizon icon, immediately paired with NOT PART OF THE LAB'S RESEARCH PROGRAMME. Centre: PRIMARY SOURCES flow into two branches. Right branch A: NEUTRON STARS -> NUMBER TO CHECK. Right branch B: GALAXY SPIN -> NO CALIBRATED TARGET (THE SOURCES GIVE NO EXPECTED SIZE FOR THE EFFECT) + NOT IDENTIFYING BY ITSELF -> ROUTE CLOSED. Animate both branches early enough that stakes, work, and verdict all land by 35 seconds.

cards.heading: “Black-hole universe” names different proposals, not one model
cards.narration: The first surprise is structural. Lana found at least five different proposals under this label—black-hole universe, or BHU for short. One identifies a closed universe with a black hole. Another says collapse rebounds—a bounce—instead of crushing to a point. Another inherits rotation. Cosmological natural selection asks whether black-hole production shapes physical constants—the fixed numbers built into physics. Other baby-universe work points to different observables. They do not share one forecast.
cards.diagram: One BHU label at upper left fans into five compact programme tiles. Each tile shows a distinct mechanism/observable glyph and a one-line label. Their output arrows terminate at different endpoints instead of converging. Do not use a cosmic montage.
on_screen_support: AT LEAST FIVE PROPOSALS IN THIS SURVEY

cards.heading: A test needs a target that can be wrong—and identify the idea
cards.narration: To test an idea, the model has to risk being wrong. It needs a number, a range, or a distinctive pattern that a measurement can miss. And the result must point back to the idea, rather than leave several possible causes. Lana found one clean numerical test in the family she surveyed. It uses neutron stars—the ultra-dense collapsed cores of exploded stars. The ones we can time as they spin are called pulsars, and their mass can be measured.
cards.diagram: Build the central logic that will recur later: MODEL -> TARGET BAND -> MEASUREMENT. First let the measurement miss the band to show CAN BE WRONG. Then let one observation point back toward several possible causes to show NOT IDENTIFYING. Finish with the two requirements: A TARGET THAT CAN BE MISSED and A RESULT THAT IDENTIFIES THE IDEA.
on_screen_support: SPINNING, TIMED NEUTRON STARS ARE PULSARS

cards.heading: One CNS chain puts a low ceiling on neutron-star mass
cards.narration: In cosmological natural selection, universes reproduce through black holes with slightly changed constants. Those constants should sit near values that favour black-hole production. In the Brown–Lee–Rho chain Lana surveyed, the Brown–Bethe maximum neutron-star mass is about one and a half times the mass of our Sun—one point five solar masses. Their paper says a neutron star at approximately two solar masses or above would put that chain in ‘serious doubt or simply falsify’ it. That is a real, falsifiable number.
cards.diagram: A restrained lineage diagram: universe -> black holes -> child universes with small parameter shifts. Transition to a horizontal neutron-star mass axis. Mark ~1.5 solar masses as Brown–Bethe maximum and shade the approximate >=2 solar-mass source regime with the exact quoted consequence SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY. No unsupported equation-of-state detail.
on_screen_support: “SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY” — BROWN, LEE & RHO

cards.heading: Measured pulsars have entered the source’s approximately two-solar-mass regime
cards.narration: Weighing a star thousands of light-years away is hard, so every measurement comes with an uncertainty range. Two pulsars reach the critical regime. Demorest's measurement is one point nine seven, plus or minus zero point zero four solar masses; its centre is below two. Fonseca's is two point zero eight, plus or minus zero point zero seven. The quoted sixty-eight point three percent interval stays above two. But at ninety-five point four percent credibility, the result does not clear two. At the quoted 68.3% level, the second measurement clears two solar masses; at the stricter 95.4% level, the packet says it does not.
cards.diagram: Full horizontal mass axis from 1.4 to 2.2 M_sun. Draw the source's ~1.5 marker and the approximate 2 M_sun regime. Row 1: Demorest 1.97 +/- 0.04, central point below 2 and interval crossing. Row 2: Fonseca 2.08 +/- 0.07 at 68.3%, with the 68.3% interval above 2. Add a separate non-scaled text callout beside the plot: "At 95.4% credibility, the packet states only that the result does not clear 2.00; no lower-bound value is quoted here." Do not draw a 95.4% endpoint, arrow, tick, bracket, or marker on the mass axis.
on_screen_support: EVERY DISTANT-STAR MASS HAS AN UNCERTAINTY RANGE
AT 95.4% CREDIBILITY, THE PACKET STATES ONLY THAT THE RESULT DOES NOT CLEAR 2.00
NO 95.4% LOWER-BOUND VALUE IS QUOTED OR PLOTTED HERE

cards.heading: The evidence enters the test regime; the packet does not call it falsification
cards.narration: This is where restraint matters. Brown, Lee, and Rho gave two possible readings, joined by an ‘or’: a heavy neutron star would put the chain in serious doubt, or simply falsify it. Lana's closing record does not decide which side applies, and neither will this video. The finding is narrower: observations have entered the regime named by the source.
cards.diagram: Keep the mass plot dimmed in the background. Place the exact source disjunction in two equal outlined boxes joined by OR. Stop a measurement arrow before either box and label PACKET DOES NOT ADJUDICATE. Highlight only ENTERS THE NAMED REGIME.

cards.heading: The rotating-parent source explicitly says the two handedness counts should differ
cards.narration: A different proposal led to our sky work. If the parent black hole rotates, the child universe inherits its axis. The source says galaxies should tend to align with that axis. It then says clockwise- and counterclockwise-spinning galaxy counts should be different. The spin lane was not chasing a phantom. It followed an explicit, source-backed qualitative claim.
cards.diagram: Simple rotating-parent cross-section, axis line passing into a child-universe circle, then a field of stylized galaxy disks aligned around that axis. Split count bins CW and CCW with an unequal sign but no invented percentage. Footer: QUALITATIVE SOURCE CLAIM · NO AMPLITUDE SHOWN.

cards.heading: The handedness claim came after the cited data and never became a numerical forecast
cards.narration: But that sentence was added in 2025, after the galaxy studies cited as support. It was not a prediction made before the data—this one came after. The paper gives equations for spinning systems, but not a numerical forecast for galaxy handedness: no expected size, no rule for how it changes with scale or redshift, no independently predicted direction, and no range that would count as a hit or a miss.
cards.diagram: Timeline: cited galaxy observations appear first; 2025 revision and its unequal-count sentence appear later. Then a forecast contract form fills MECHANICS present but leaves four red outlined blanks: SIZE, SCALE/REDSHIFT LAW, INDEPENDENT DIRECTION, ACCEPTANCE RANGE. Avoid saying the source contains no numbers or equations.
on_screen_support: NOT A PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THE DATA
NO EXPECTED SIZE OR PASS-OR-FAIL RANGE FOR HANDEDNESS

cards.heading: A real spin difference would still not identify a black-hole origin
cards.narration: Suppose a controlled survey found a real spin-handedness difference. That would be interesting. But that broad observation would not identify BHU by itself. One observed number would have more than one possible interpretation unless a BHU model supplied a unique signature. A successful measurement is not automatically a successful test of this model.
cards.diagram: The centerpiece identifying-test diagram. One observed node, CW/CCW DIFFERENCE, points backward toward BHU? and OTHER POSSIBLE CAUSES. The backward arrow splits, so the observation cannot select one cause. Do not name or depict specific rival cosmologies. End on the explicit logic MEASUREMENT ≠ IDENTIFICATION.

cards.heading: The spin route fails twice: no numerical target, and no unique signature
cards.narration: The route therefore fails in two independent ways. A finite-precision spin result cannot be scored against a source-defined pass-or-fail range, because the source gives no predicted size. And without a unique signature, a positive result cannot identify BHU. We could build a trustworthy measurement and still be unable to answer the BHU question. The hunt had a source. It did not have a target.
cards.diagram: Two-column fail-closed ledger. Column A: NO SOURCE-DEFINED PASS-OR-FAIL RANGE—show a finite-precision spin result beside a blank scoring ruler labelled NO PREDICTED SIZE; do not imply that every possible qualitative observation is irrelevant. Column B: NO UNIQUE SIGNATURE—show one observed node with split backward arrows labelled POSITIVE RESULT DOES NOT IDENTIFY BHU. Both columns feed ROUTE CLOSED FOR THIS CAMPAIGN'S SKY-STATISTICS LINE. Keep MEASUREMENT MAY STILL BE TRUSTWORTHY visibly separate. Final line: THE HUNT HAD A SOURCE · IT DID NOT HAVE A TARGET.
on_screen_support: A FINITE-PRECISION RESULT CANNOT BE NUMERICALLY SCORED AGAINST A RANGE THE SOURCE DOES NOT GIVE
A POSITIVE RESULT DOES NOT IDENTIFY BHU
THE HUNT HAD A SOURCE · IT DID NOT HAVE A TARGET

cards.heading: Reopen this route only for a calibrated target or a unique signature
cards.narration: What would change the verdict? First, a published calculation connecting parent-black-hole parameters to a handedness amplitude, scale, or redshift dependence, with a pass-or-fail range. Or second, a fingerprint only a black-hole birth would leave—not merely the broad fact of spin asymmetry. A confirmed spin asymmetry alone would still not test BHU. This route reopens only when a BHU model supplies a calibrated target or a unique signature.

A standalone CONFIRMED SPIN ASYMMETRY token approaches but cannot unlock either gate. Finish with both requirements and the heading held alone long enough to read; no caveat or credit card follows.
